content: White marks, also known as white spot lesions, often appear on teeth after braces are removed. These marks are an early sign of tooth decay, or dental caries, and are seen in approximately 25% of orthodontic patients. White spot lesions result from the demineralization of enamel, which occurs when plaque accumulates on the tooth surface. If left untreated, these lesions can progress to cavities. Additionally, orthodontic treatment is frequently associated with swollen, bleeding gums, a sign of gingivitis, which is an early stage of gum disease. The development of dental caries and periodontal disease requires the simultaneous presence of four factors: saliva, bacteria, a suitable substrate (such as sugar), and a tooth surface or periodontal tissue. These factors create an environment conducive to bacterial growth, leading to the formation of dental plaque. Plaque is the primary cause of both gingivitis and dental caries. Effective plaque removal through good oral hygiene is essential to prevent these conditions. Orthodontic patients, particularly those with fixed braces, face increased challenges in maintaining oral hygiene. The brackets and wires of fixed appliances create additional surfaces for plaque to accumulate, making it more difficult to clean teeth effectively. This increased plaque retention heightens the risk of enamel demineralization and gum inflammation. Toothbrushing is widely regarded as an effective method for removing plaque and preventing demineralization. However, it is unclear whether using a manual toothbrush alone is sufficient for optimal plaque removal in orthodontic patients. Some experts recommend the use of interdental or interspace brushes to clean hard-to-reach areas, such as the spaces between teeth and around brackets. Studies have shown that interdental brushes can effectively reduce plaque in these areas, particularly in patients with interdental spaces, periodontal pockets, or dental bridges. However, other research suggests that using interdental brushes in addition to a manual toothbrush may not provide significant benefits compared to using a manual toothbrush alone. Various adjunctive tools have been developed to improve oral hygiene in orthodontic patients. These include curved-bristle toothbrushes, triple-headed toothbrushes, orthodontic toothbrushes, and other toothbrush adaptations. Technological devices, such as sonic toothbrushes, dental water jets with orthodontic tips, and electric interdental cleaning devices, have also been explored. Traditional cleaning tools, such as the Siwak or Miswak, have been studied as well. While some evidence supports the effectiveness of these tools, there is limited research on their use in patients with conventional fixed braces. For example, triple-headed toothbrushes have been shown to be effective for patients with lingually placed fixed appliances, but their efficacy for more common fixed appliances remains unclear. This review aims to evaluate all mechanical cleaning interventions for orthodontic patients with fixed appliances. Adolescents are the primary focus, as they represent the largest group undergoing orthodontic treatment. However, age is not expected to influence the outcomes, and participants of all ages with acceptable oral hygiene at the start of treatment will be considered. Patients with disabilities that prevent them from maintaining good oral hygiene will be excluded, as they are unlikely to begin fixed appliance treatment. While changing oral hygiene habits can improve oral health, recent research has focused on strategies to enhance adherence to oral hygiene instructions in orthodontic patients. Although this area is beyond the scope of this review, it highlights the importance of patient compliance. Other measures, such as the use of MI Paste Plus (a remineralizing agent), have shown promise in reducing demineralization but are not considered mechanical cleaning methods and will not be included in this review. Effective plaque removal is critical to preventing white spot lesions, demineralization, and the progression to caries or gum disease. Patients who complete orthodontic treatment with permanent tooth marks or gum disease are likely to be dissatisfied with their results. Providing evidence-based guidance on maintaining oral hygiene during treatment is essential for both patients and professionals. While interdental brushes are effective, they require time and dexterity, which may not be practical for all patients. Newer technological tools may offer more efficient solutions. If these tools prove ineffective, relying solely on a standard toothbrush could save patients time, money, and the effort of learning additional skills. This review seeks to provide definitive recommendations for maintaining oral hygiene in orthodontic patients with fixed appliances.
